<header>Beschrijvinghe van Lima/ stadt der Coninghen.</header>

<margin>
Ghedaente van de stadt Lima.
</margin>
Indese stadt zijn goede huysen/ en die sommi-ge seer schoone met toornkens en galerijen. Het merckt velt is groot/ ende die straten breet/ alle recht op de merct aencomende/ van waer men oock in alle hoecke sien mach/ en ten beyden zy-den het vlack velt/ en door 't meeste deel van die huysen gaen Canalen uyt/ die Reviere versch water aenbrengende/ en seer groote commoditeyt en gerieffelijcheyt der Borgheren/ moghen hier door alle hare bogaerde en kruythoven begie-ten/ die zy schoon en genoechlijck hebben. Oock 

<margin>
Vele Water-molens/ waer mede zy haer Coren malen.
</margin>
so liggen in dese Reviere veel water molens op onse landts aert/ daer zy haer Coren op malē/ in somma hier woonen seer rijcke borgers/ die sommighe 150. duyfent ducatē hebben. En van dese stadt varen ten tyden schepē 800. duyfent ducaten waerdich/ en noch sommighe van een millioen. Aen die oost zyde/ boven in die stadt is een hooge bergh/ waer op een Cruyfix staet. Aen een ander zyde buyten die stadt hebbe die Borgeren hare wooningen en plaetsen daer zp die besten houde/ ende haer duyf huysen/ hare Wijngaerde/ doch geen goede druyven/ om die aert des landts/ schoone hoven/ niet alleen vol van allerley vruchten van dat landt: maer ooc 

<margin>
Beschrijvinge der vrucht-baerheyt des landts.
</margin>
van die spaensche/ als Vygen/ Granaten/ Limoenē/ Citroenē/ Orangen/ Meloenē/ Boonen/ Erwitten en Suycker rieden/ alle seer smackelijck/ jae beter dā in spaengien/ en voor-waer om het menschelijcke levē met vreuchde te passeren/ als die schandale oneenicheden en oorloge daer niet en ware/ is voorseker dese plaetse een van die schoonste van die geheele werelt: want die landtschap daer ontret so getepere/ dat het geheele jaer over geen excessive hitte ofte schadelijcke koude daer is/ oock heeft men nopt gesien dat daer honger ofte pest/ ofte eenige regen ofte donderflagen/ ofte blixem vanden Hemel 

<margin>
Waer voor de Coningen kade haren naem vercregen heeft/ en is ghebout int jaer 1535.
</margin>
geslagen: maer ter contrarie altoos eē helder/ klare en schoone Hemel/ is gesticht van de Admirael Don Francisco Pizarro, int jaer 1535. is genaēt der Coningē stadt/ om dat het volck op drie Coningen dagh/ daer in gebracht zijn/ aenlangēde listrocht/ behalven die visch/ die zy uyt die Zee ende Reviere in grooter overvloet hebbe/ als oock vleysch en vruchte der boomen en der aerde/ gelijck gesept is/ niet minder isser vor overvloedich Terwe en greyn/ en die vier maende alst in spaengiē somer is/ so ist aldaer winter/ ende een wepnich kouder als op ander tijt. In dese 4. winters maende valt alle daghe voor dē middagh eē kleyne dou ofte mist ghelpck nevel/ doch niet als by ons ongesont: wat die welcke pyne int hooft hebbe/ haer hier mede wasschende/ krygen verlichtinghe. Is seer apparent/ dat dese stadt Lima dagelijcks meer toe neme sal van volck en rijckdō/ hoe wel daer voor veel jaren over die 500. huysen gheweest 

<margin>
De breede en lenghte der huysen van Lima.
</margin>
hebben/ en die stadt is seer wit ghebout/ datter wel 2000 staē mogen/ want die straten breedt zijn/ en dat merckt velt groot/ elck huys heeft 80. voete erfs/ en 160. voeten lengten. En om datter geen bequaem hout en is om solders af te maken: want wort binnen 2. ofte 3. jarē vā die wormen veretelt/ so huysen niet dan van eene verdiepinge gebout/ noch tās zeer 

<margin>
Ghedaente vande huysen
</margin>
kostelijck en magnifijck met vele cameren/ salē en faletten/ bequaem om te woone/ en vreemde gasten te herbergen: Die wanden zijn gemaect van eenige materialen die zy aen malkanderen backe seer dick/ en vullē die met aerde. Op decken hare huysen met gheschilderde matten/ oft geschildert lijnwaet/ ronds omme en bovē

<column-break/>

op die wanden make zy prieelkens van riepen daer zy in schuylen voor die Sonne. Voor den regen doze zy niet sorgē: wat ten regent daer niet. Dese stadt heeft onder haer alle dese stede daer Bisschoppen woonen/ Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trugillo, Guanuco, Chachapoia, Portus vetus, Guayaquil, Popaian, Catchi, S. Michael, S. Francisco. Hier bevorens is gesept dat Peru afgedeelt wordt in drierley landtschappen. In plat lādt aen die Zee in bergen ofte berghachtich landt midden door Peru loopende/ en in landt over die gheberchten. Van het platte landt/ aen die oever des Meers hebben wp tot noch gehandelt/ beginnende vā die Linea eñ die C. Passao tot hier toe/ so is noch te weten/ dat van Tumbes af niet alleen tot Lima: maer noch veel verder die Zee Cust zupden op zeer drooch ende vol groote woeste sandt plaetsen is/ daer 't op 10. mylen weghes die stadt dondert/ bliremt noch regent: maer over die 10. myle wel/ ofte so veel mūn ofte meer alst gheberchte van die Zee lept: Daer zijn oock in dit platte landt geen fonteynen ofte putte: maer wel 4. ofte 5. staende wateren die brack zijn/ om dat zp nae bp die Zee ligghen. Die Inwoonders onderhouden haer met het water uyt die Reviere/ die van die geberchte comen/ die door de sneeu en regē die in de bergē vallen oorspronck nemē/ niet uyt fonteynen die wepnich int gheberchte zijn. Die distantie deser Revieren zijn eensdeels hier te bevores beschrevē/ liggē 7. 8. 10. 12. 15. en 20. mplē vande anderē/ doch meest 7. ofte 8. waer na die repsende lupde haer regulerē/ om dat zp geē ander water elders vindē. Ten bepde zpdē vā dese revierē/ een mple weeghs breet/ ofte ooc luyder/ somtyts meer/ somtyts min/ nae die gelegentheyt vant landt/ zijn differente vrucht-bare boome en coren landen die vant volck gebouwt en besaept werden/ 'twelck zp het gheheele jaer over doen moghen; Oock wassen ontrent dese revierē veellerlep wilde boome/ Cotton/ Riet/ Distelen/ Biesen eñ Lis/ etc. En nae dat die Spaengiaerden het landt inghenomen hebbe/ saepen ooc Terwe/ die landt vocht makende door eenighe Canalen die zp uyt dese Revieren leyden/ Welcke om dat zp van hooghe bergen snel af loopen/ datmen qualijck sonder hulpe over varen mach/ en veel daer inne ver-droncken. Die langs het platte land hare repse doen/ houden gemeenlijck so dichte aen die Zee kant/ dat zp die altoos int gesichte hebbe. Alst winter int geberchte is en veel regent/ so ist periculooz daer te reysen/ om 't aenloopen der revieren die men passeren moet/ ofte met seeckere vloten die zp daer toe hebben/ ofte met een net dat zp met Cauwaerden dichte vullen/ daer op die repsende man uptegestreckt moet liggen/ en eender van die Indianen swemt voren/ dat net ofte die blote met een coorde voort treckende/ en een ander vā achter stuerēde. Het volck vant platte landt woonē onder hutten van mepē gemaeckt. Die mans dragen hemde en doecken op die knien en daer over streckēde/ eñ opperste kleet gelijck eē mantel. Die vrouwē ee Cours vā Cottoen nae die lengte des lijfs/ en hoe wel 't fatsoē van die cleedinge vast over al eenderlep is/ so isser nochtans eenich onderschept int pareelsel des hoofts: wat sommighe enckele coodekē/ sommighe gevlochte/ eenige vā eederlep/ andere van verschepden coleuren die dragē/ en niemant isser ofte hy draecht pet op t hooft/ en alle onderschepdē/ na gewoonhept des landts.
Dese

reference_text: In this towne are faire houses, some built with Towers and costly galleries: the Market place is great, and the streetes broade, and entring into the market place, from whence also you may goe into everie place of the towne, and to the fieldes, and into most of the houses there runneth certain channels that convay water, a great commoditie and pleasure unto the townesmen, wherewith they may water all their gardens and orchards, which are there verie faire and pleasant: upon the river likewise are many water milles, made after the manner of our countrey, wherewith they grinde their corne, to conclude, therein dwelleth many rich inhabitants, some worth 150000. duckets: and from this towne oftentimes there saileth shippes that are worth in value at the least 800000. duckets, and some a Million: on the east side a little above the towne, lyeth a high hill, whereon there standeth a Crucifix: on another side of the towne, the townsmen have certaine places where they keepe their cattell, their dovehouses, vineyards, (but no good grapes because of the grounde) gardens of pleasure, not onely full of all those countrie fruits, but also of Spanish fruites, as figges, poungarnats, lemons, oranges, melons, beanes, pease, and sugar canes, all verie good and savorie, and better then in Spaine, and to say the truth, to passe a mans life in quietnesse (were it not for the reporte that runneth of the Spaniards, that they make warre against those people without a cause) I thinke it the best and most pleasant place in all the world, the aire being so temperate, that all the yeare long there is no extremitie either of heate or cold, and it was never heard that ever they had famine, plague, or any raine, thunder, or lightning, but to the contrarie, alwayes a cleare and faire skie: it was builded by the Admirall Don Francisco Pizarro in the yeare of our Lord 1535. and was called the Kings towne, because they arrived therein upon twelfe day, by us so called. Touching victualles, besides fish, which they have both out of the sea and the River, in great aboundance, as also flesh and fruits of trees, and of the earth, as I saide before: they have no lesse quantitie of wheate: and the foure moneths of summer in Spaine, are winter with them, onely somewhat colder then the summer: in those foure moneths of winter, there falleth everie day in the forenoone, a small dew or mist, but not unholsome, as with us, for that those that have any paine in their heades, washing their heades therewith, it healeth the ach: it is verie likelie that this towne of Lima will daily increase in people and houses, for many yeares together there were not above 500. houses therein, yet the place is great inough to containe 2000. houses, for the streetes are verie broade, and the market as bigge as a great fielde, everie house is eightie foote broade, and a hundred and sixtie foote long, and because there is no convenient woodde whereof to make chambers, for that all their wood within two or three yeares is cleane consumed by wormes, therefore the houses be but of one storie high, yet verie costly and sumptuous, with many chambers, halles, and parlers, both fitte to dwell in, and also to receive strangers, the walles of the houses are made of a certaine stuffe baked hard together, and filled with earth. They cover their houses with painted mattes, or else with painted linnen, and round about and above uppon the walles they make arbours of greene boughes, wherein they sit to keepe themselves from the sunne, for raine they neede not care, for there it never raineth: this Citie hath under it al these townes hereafter named, where there are Bishops, as Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trugillo, Guanuco, Chachapoia, Portus Verus, Guaiaquil, Popaian, Carchi, Saint Michael, and S. Francis. Before it was saide that Peru is divided into three provinces, in flat or plaine land, on the sea coast in hillie lande, that runneth through the middle of Peru, and in other lands, lying beyonde the hilles: touching the flat lande on the sea shore, I have hitherto spoken, beginning from the line, and the Cape Passao hitherto, so you must understand that from Tumbez, not onelie to Lima but also further southward, the sea coast is full of many great droughts, and wilde sandie places, where for the space of ten miles it never thundereth lightneth, nor raineth, but beyonde that, or all the space that is betweene those tenne miles and the hilles, it thundereth, lightneth, and raineth. In this flatte land there are no fountaines nor welles, but foure or five standing waters that are brackish, because they are neare the sea, the inhabitants use the river waters, that run out of the hilles, which spring of the snow and raine that falleth on the hilles, and not out of fountaines that stande among the hils. The distance of these rivers are alreadie partly described, lying seven, eight, ten, twelve, fifteene, and twentie miles one from the other, yet most part seven or eight, whereby such as travaile direct their course, because they have no other waters: on both sides of these rivers about a mile broade or further, and sometimes more or lesse, according to the scituation of the countrey, are divers fruitfull trees, and corne landes, which are planted and sowed by the people of the countrey, which they may do all the yeare long, also there groweth about those rivers many wilde trees, cotten, reeds, thistles, and Lis, and since the Spaniards subdued the countrey, they sowe wheate, moystning the lands by certaine channels, made out of the Rivers, and because they runne with so great force out of the high hilles, that without helpe men can hardly passe them, and many are drowned: such as travaile in that flat countrey go so neare to the sea coast, that they have them alwayes in their sight: when it is winter in the hilles, and that it raineth much, it is dangerous travailing in those countries, specially to passe the rivers, which they must either do upon drifts which they have for the purpose, or with a net, which they fill with canwoorden or gourds, whereupon the travailer must lie, and one of the Indians swimmeth before him, drawing the net or drift, and an other behinde that steereth it. The people in the flat land dwell in houses made of boughes, the men weare shirts and cloathes uppon their knees, and over it they cast an upper garment or mantle, the women weare a kinde of cotten pettiecoate, from the head to the foote, and although their manner of apparrel is in everie place almost alike, yet they use certain differences in the attiring of their heades, some wearing nothing but plaine hairelaces, some double and wreathed, others of one colour, and some of divers colours, and there is no man but he weareth some thing uppon his head, and all different, according to the manner of the country.

<meta>This page continues the description of the Peruvian coast, moving from the travel route to a detailed account of Lima, the colonial capital, its architecture, climate, and the surrounding geography of the "Llanos" (flat lands).</meta>

# Description of Lima, City of the Kings.

<margin>
The appearance of the city of Lima.
</margin>
In this city, there are good houses, some of which are very beautiful with small towers and galleries. The market square is large, and the streets are wide, all leading directly to the market, from where one may also see into every corner; on both sides lies the open field. Through most of the houses run canals, bringing fresh water from the river, providing great convenience and comfort for the citizens, who can thereby water all their orchards and herb gardens, which they keep beautiful and pleasant. Also,

<margin>
Many watermills, with which they grind their grain.
</margin>
in this river lie many watermills after our own country’s fashion <note>The author compares them to Dutch-style mills</note>, where they grind their grain. In short, very wealthy citizens live here, some of whom possess 150,000 ducats. From this city, ships sometimes depart carrying cargo worth 800,000 ducats, and some even worth a million. On the east side, above the city, is a high mountain upon which stands a crucifix. On another side outside the city, the citizens have their dwellings and places where they keep their livestock, as well as their dovecotes and their vineyards—though the grapes are not good due to the nature of the soil. They have beautiful gardens, filled not only with all kinds of fruits of that land, but also

<margin>
Description of the fertility of the land.
</margin>
with those from Spain, such as figs, pomegranates, lemons, citrons, oranges, melons, beans, peas, and sugarcanes, all very tasty—indeed, better than in Spain. Truly, for passing a human life with joy—were it not for the scandalous discords and wars—this place is certainly one of the most beautiful in the whole world. For the landscape there is so temperate that throughout the entire year there is no excessive heat or harmful cold. Moreover, it has never been seen that hunger or plague occurred there, nor any rain, thunderclaps, or lightning from Heaven

<margin>
Why the City of the Kings obtained its name, and was built in the year 1535.
</margin>
striking the earth. On the contrary, there is always a clear, bright, and beautiful sky. It was founded by the Admiral Don Francisco Pizarro in the year 1535 and is named the City of the Kings because the people were brought into it on Epiphany <note>original: *drie Coningen dagh*; literally "Three Kings' Day," January 6th</note>. Regarding provisions, besides the fish which they have in great abundance from the sea and the river, as well as meat and the fruits of the trees and the earth, as has been said, there is no less an abundance of wheat and grain. During the four months when it is summer in Spain, it is winter there, being a little colder than at other times. In these four winter months, a small dew or mist like a fog falls every day before noon, yet it is not unhealthy like ours; those who have a pain in the head find relief by washing themselves with it. It is very apparent that this city of Lima will daily increase in population and wealth, although for many years there have been over 500 houses,

<margin>
The width and length of the houses of Lima.
</margin>
and the city is built so white that it might well contain 2,000, for the streets are wide and the market square large. Each house has a lot 80 feet wide and 160 feet long. And because there is no suitable wood to make upper floors—for within two or three years it is consumed by worms <note>Likely termites or wood-boring beetles</note>—the houses are built with only one story. Nevertheless, they are very

<margin>
Appearance of the houses.
</margin>
costly and magnificent, with many rooms, halls, and galleries <note>original: *faletten*; likely refers to architectural features like loggias or balconies</note>, suitable for living and for lodging foreign guests. The walls are made of certain materials that they bake together very thickly and fill with earth. They cover their houses with painted mats or painted linen; all around and above

<column-break/>

on the walls, they make small arbors of hoops <note>original: *prieelkens van riepen*</note> where they take shelter from the sun. They do not need to worry about rain, for it does not rain there. This city has jurisdiction over all these cities where Bishops reside: Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trujillo, Guanuco, Chachapoia, Portus Vetus, Guayaquil, Popayan, Catchi, St. Michael, and St. Francisco. It was mentioned previously that Peru is divided into three types of landscapes: the flat land by the sea, the mountains or mountainous land running through the middle of Peru, and the land beyond the mountains. Of the flat land on the shore of the sea, we have dealt until now, starting from the Equator <note>original: *Linea*</note> and Cape Passao to this point. It should also be known that from Tumbes not only to Lima, but much further south, the sea coast is very dry and full of large, desolate sandy places. Within ten miles of the city, it never thunders, lightens, nor rains; but beyond those ten miles—or as far as the mountains lie from the sea—it does. There are also no springs or wells in this flat land, but rather four or five standing waters that are brackish because they lie near the sea. The inhabitants support themselves with water from the rivers that come from the mountains, which originate from the snow and rain that fall in the mountains, not from springs, of which there are few in the mountains. The distances between these rivers were partly described before; they lie 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, and 20 miles from each other, but mostly 7 or 8, by which travelers regulate their journey because they find no other water elsewhere. On both sides of these rivers, for a mile’s breadth or sometimes more, sometimes less, depending on the layout of the land, there are various fruitful trees and grain fields which are cultivated and sown by the people; this they may do throughout the entire year. Also, many types of wild trees grow around these rivers: cotton, reeds, thistles, rushes, and irises, etc. And since the Spaniards took the land, they also sow wheat, making the land moist through certain canals <note>The *acequias* or irrigation channels inherited from the Incas and expanded by Spaniards</note> which they lead out of these rivers. Because these rivers run swiftly down from high mountains, one can hardly cross them without help, and many have drowned in them. Those who make their journey along the flat land generally keep so close to the seaside that they always have it in sight. When it is winter in the mountains and rains heavily, it is perilous to travel there because of the rising of the rivers that one must pass, either by certain floats they have for that purpose, or with a net that they fill tightly with gourds <note>original: *Cauwaerden*; calabashes used as flotation devices</note>, upon which the traveler must lie stretched out; one of the Indians swims in front, pulling the net or float with a cord, and another steers from behind. The people of the flat land live in huts made of branches. The men wear shirts and cloths reaching to the knees, and over that an upper garment like a mantle. The women wear a gown of cotton the length of the body; and although the fashion of the clothing is almost the same everywhere, there is nonetheless some distinction in the head-dressing: for some wear a single small cord, some braided, some of one color, others of various colors, and there is no one who does not wear something on the head, all distinguished according to the custom of the land.
This

<margin>

<header>GEZANDTSCHAP aan den Grooten</header>
<meta>catchword: Daar</meta>

<margin>Dat de Sinefche Raats-heeren op negen brengen.</margin>
Tot dit gevoelen neigden al d'andere Tartarifche Raats-heeren; maar de Sineefche Raats-heeren gelieten zich als of zy den Hollanders noch grooter gunste wilden toedragen, en dreven, dat men de zelve niet als om de negen jaren behoorde wederom te laten komen; dewijl men hen anders door de verheit der reize te veel in de waagh-schaal zou stellen. Dan zy hadden hier een achter-deur open, die de Tartarifche Raats-heeren niet gemerkt hadden, en verstonden dat de Hollanders midlerwijle in *Kanton* niet zouden mogen komen handelen. Zy gaven den Raat wijders in bedenken, of onder schijn van Hollanders niet wel Engelschen mochten schuilen; met by-brengen, dat d'Engelschen over dertig jaren met vier Schepen in de haven van *Heytamon* Zout-Jonken hadden aangehaalt, den Mandarijn gevangen genomen, een Sterkte om verre geschoten, en voorts zoodanige vuile dingen bedreven, datze van dien tijdt af voor vyanden van den Staat verklaart en gehouden waren, en ook toen besloten was, dat de Engelsche noit na dien tijdt in *Sina* zouden ingelaten worden; invoegge men nader proeve en beter bescheit van d'oprechtigheid der Hollanders moste hebben, voor al eer zy in 't Rijk ingelaten wierden. Want behalve het met de gewoonte streed, dat hen de vrye handel in 't Rijk wiert toegestaan, zoo kon men ook niet vernemen dat het zelve in de geloof-brieven der Gezanten verzocht wiert; zulks zy daar uit vermoeden dat de Gezanten buiten hun last gingen. Wonder vreemt quam dit den Gezanten te vore, en was hen een donderslagh in d'ooren zulks te hooren; gemerkt zy tot noch toe geen andere gedachten hadden gehad, of de Keizer had, volgens den inhout van den tweeden last-brief, hier bevorens by de Onder-koningen van *Kanton* bekoomen, het verzoek der Hollanders, nopende den vryen handel in *Kanton*, volkomentlijk toegestaan, en dat zy alleenlijk zijne Majesteit daar over in *Peking* zouden koomen bedanken. Zy konden wel begrijpen, dat Pater Adam en noch twee andere Jesuiten, die al-

<margin>Die ook willen en zeggen dat de Hollanders Engelsche zijn.</margin>

<margin>De Jesuiten zijn de Gezanten ook hinderlijk.</margin>

<column-break/>

daar woonachtigh waren, ontrent drie hondert teil Zilvers (om den voortgang van dit werk te beletten) verspilt, en noch meer belooft hadden; als ook datze de Tarters hadden wijsgemaakt, dat de Hollanders, onder dek-mantel van te handelen, niet anders zochten, dan voor eerst eenen voet in 't Lant te krijgen, en daar na te roven wat zy konden meê-slepen. Hen quam ook ter ooren, hoe deze drie Jesuiten geweldigh geklaaght hadden, dat *Makao* door dezen handel t'eenemaal zou verarmen. Dat daar en boven het aanbrengen van den Commissaris, die over drie Jaren in *Kanton* was geweest, als ook het schrijven van den *Tutang*, die als toen noch in *Kanton* zich bevond, en te dien tijde van die van *Makao* met zilver omgekocht was, aldaar zulk een gevoelen in de harten van velen gebracht had, dat men hen niet anders hield, dan voor een deel t'zamen-gerodt volk, dat geen lant had, en zich alleenlijk met rooven en andere ongeoorlofde middelen, inzonderheidt ter Zee, erneerde, konden de Gezanten noch wel vatten en bevroeden; maar dat de Rijx-cancellier en andere Raden (om den zin van deze woorden, *te mogen gaan en keeren*, in de geloofnis-Brieven der Gezanten vervat, en daar meê niet anders betekent wiert, als *te mogen handelen*, aan den Keizer uit te leggen en te verklaren) met gelt mosten worden omgekocht, quam hen wonder vreemt te voore; nadien zy niet beter wisten, of de vijf en dertigh hondert teil Zilvers (die zy by Schult-brief aan de Kantonsche Onder-koningen, op hen aangewezen, aldaar te dien einde belooft hadden te betalen) waren aan de Rijx-raden verdeelt en uitgeschooten. Als zy derhalven bevonden, dat de zelve Onder-koningen hen hier in hadden bedroogen, wierden zy gedwongen na andere middelen uit te zien, om tot hun oogh-merk te geraken. Zy stelden dan voor eerst ter vergaderingh, van den tweeden Rijx-cancellier te dien einde beleidt, het punt van den Jaarlixzen handel in *Kanton* in perzoone en duidelijk voor, en hielden daar op aan om dien te verkrijgen.

[context] Afterwards the Chancellour Summoned the Tartar and China Councils together, to consider of the Proposals of the Hollanders, alledging (he being President) that they ought to give them leave every fifth year to come and salute the Emperour:
most of the Tartars were of this opinion, but the Chineses seemed outwardly willing to show far greater favour to the Hollanders, namely, that they should come but once every nine years to Peking, by reason of the vast distance from Batavia to the Imperial City. But herein they thought to have out-witted the Tartars, for they understood that the Hollanders were not to be permitted in the mean time to Trade at Canton. They proposed also to the Assembly, whether under the notion of Hollanders, the English might not likewise appear, who about thirty years since came with four Ships into the Harbour of Heytamon, where they took away four Vessels laden with Salt, the Mandarine Prisoner, and shot down a Fort, committing several other violences, for which from that time they were held and declared Enemies of the Empire; therefore they should be satisfied of the Integrity of the Hollanders, before they were permitted to Trade in China: For beside that it was contrary to the custom of the Countrey to let them have a Free Trade in any part of the Empire, neither did it appear by their Credentials that any such thing was desired; so that they concluded that they had exceeded their orders.
The Embassadours were not a little surprized at these proceedings of the Council, for they understood no otherwise, but that the Emperour had according to the Contents of the second Mandatory Letter, formerly procured by the Vice-Roy of Canton, fully agreed to the request of the Hollanders concerning a Free Trade in Canton; and that they had only thereupon to go and return their thanks to his Majesty at Peking. The Embassadours were well enough informed of the designs and practices of Father Adam and some other Jesuites, who had lived there [many] years, and had been bribed under hand by the Portuguesses, to oppose the Hollanders in this their design of Free Commerce in China; therefore they endeavoured to perswade the Tartars, that the Hollanders under colour and pretence of Merchandizing, designed nothing less but to get footing first of all in their Countrey, and afterwards to Plunder and carry away whatsoever was Portable. The Embassadours were also informed how that these Jesuits had likewise highly complained, that Maccao would be utterly ruined and impoverished by such a Trade, and withal that they had told the Tartars, to make them the more averse to the Hollanders, that they were a people made up of several Nations, without any Habitations, and only subsisted by Pyracy at Sea. But that which most of all surprized the Embassadours, was to find themselves deceived of their Money by the Canton Vice-Roys, to whom they had paid thirty five hundred Toel of Silver; which sum the Vice-Roys promised to pay the Chancellour and some others of his Majesties Council, to procure their favour and assistance for a dispatch of their [business]: but finding that they were [deceived] by the Vice-Roys, they were forced to consider of some other way to obtain their purpose: wherefore they first thought good to propose to the Council the point of coming to trade yearly at Canton, and to endeavour to effect the same [...].

# EMBASSY to the Great
<meta>catchword: There</meta>

<margin>That the Chinese Councilors propose nine [years].</margin>
All the other Tartar Councilors inclined toward this opinion; but the Chinese Councilors acted as if they wished to show the Dutch even greater favor, and insisted that one ought not let them return except every nine years; since one would otherwise expose them to too much risk through the distance of the journey. Yet they had a back door open here, which the Tartar Councilors had not noticed, and they intended that the Dutch should not be allowed to come and trade in *Canton* in the meantime. They further put it to the council to consider whether, under the guise of being Dutch, there might not be English hiding; bringing up that thirty years ago, the English had approached Salt-Jonks in the harbor of *Heytamon* with four ships, taken the Mandarin prisoner, shot down a fortress, and furthermore committed such foul things that from that time on they were declared and held as enemies of the State, and it was also decided then that the English should never after that be admitted into *China*; whereby one must have further proof and better information of the sincerity of the Dutch before they were admitted into the Realm. For besides that it went against custom that they were granted free trade in the Realm, one could also not discern that it was requested in the letters of credence of the Envoys; such that they suspected from this that the Envoys were exceeding their instructions. Very strangely did this appear to the Envoys, and it was a thunderclap in their ears to hear this; noted that they had had no other thoughts until now but that the Emperor, according to the content of the second mandate previously obtained from the Viceroys of *Canton*, had completely granted the request of the Dutch regarding free trade in *Canton*, and that they were only to come to thank his Majesty for it in *Peking*. They could well understand that Father Adam and two other Jesuits, who were resident there, had wasted about three hundred *tael* of silver (to prevent the progress of this work) and had promised even more; as also that they had made the Tartars believe that the Dutch, under the cloak of trading, were seeking nothing else than to get a foot in the country first, and thereafter to steal whatever they could carry away with them. It also came to their ears how these three Jesuits had complained violently that *Macau* would become completely impoverished by this trade. That, furthermore, the denunciation by the Commissioner who had been in *Canton* three years prior, as well as the writing of the *Tutang* <note>A high-ranking provincial governor</note>, who was still in *Canton* at that time and had been bribed with silver by those of *Macau*, had brought such an opinion into the hearts of many that one held them to be nothing more than a band of gathered-up people who had no land, and earned their living only by stealing and other illicit means, especially at sea; this the Envoys could well grasp and surmise. But that the Chancellor of the Realm and other Councilors had to be bribed with money (to explain and interpret the meaning of these words, *to be allowed to come and go*, contained in the letters of credence, as *to be allowed to trade*) to the Emperor, seemed very strange to them; since they knew no better than that the thirty-five hundred *tael* of silver (which they had promised to pay there for that purpose by a promissory note addressed to the Viceroys of *Canton*) had been distributed among and paid out to the Councilors of the Realm. When they therefore discovered that the same Viceroys had deceived them in this, they were forced to look for other means to reach their goal. They then proposed, first of all, at the assembly managed to that end by the second Chancellor of the Realm, the point of the annual trade in *Canton* in person and clearly, and insisted upon obtaining it.

<header>Gedenkwaerdig Gesandtschap</header>
<sig>Ss</sig>
<meta>catchword: donne</meta>

*Schaap* en *Byleveldt* merkten nu waar 't aan haperde, dat *Tofaymon* en *Manyckebe* zich zoo afgezondert hielden van de *Hollanders*, en haar alleenlyk toe-fnaauwden: Gy-luiden praat uwe monden mis voor de rechters. Waarom dieshalven ootmoedig verzochten: of *Kytsbyoye*, *Phatfyofaymon* en *Syovan*, die nu de zaak recht vatteden, de moeite wilden neemen, om wegens de gezeide mis-flag, by de Nederduitfche tolken begaan, den heer *Sicungodonne* te begroeten: welk verzoek alle drie zeer ernfthaftigh aannamen. Vertrekkende, gaven den *Hollanders* goeden moed.

<margin>Onderhandeling der tolken onder malkander.</margin>
En de zaak fcheen haar waarlyk ter herten te gaan, alzoo des anderen daags wederom in de Hollandtfche herbergh verfcheenen: alwaar *Manyckebe* vonden: dien zy te gemoet voerden: hoe hy, en byzonder *Tofaymon*, de *Hollanders* voor de Ryks-raaden fantfch qualyk had vertolkt: 't was hoog-noodigh dat *Manyckebe* zyn fpits-broeder *Tofaymon* dieswegen begroete. Doch *Manyckebe* wees het af: alzoo *Tofaymon* opper-tolk was, voor wien zwichten moeft. Echter het quam *Tofaymon* ter ooren: die niet verflofte den *Hollanders* over de quade vertaaling aan te fpreeken. Hy verontfchuldigde zich, dat niet de fchorting by hem, maar by *Sicungodonne* was: alzoo getrouwelyk woord voor woord vertolkt hadde: daar nochtans *Sicungodonne* de zelve zomtyds geheel anders aan de Ryks-raaden over bragt, als gezeid wierden. Ondertuffchen bleek genoeghzaam by *Tofaymons* gebaerten, dat niet buiten fchuld ftond. *Schaap* dieshalven verzocht: hy beliefde voor het toekomende onderzoek doch goede zorge te dragen omtrent de vragen en antwoorden: ten einde de Japanfche Overigheid moght geraken aan de waare gefchapenheit der zaak, en zy *Hollanders* in geen vordere hapering. Hy beloofde zulks te zullen na komen, en vertrok.

<margin>Hollanders waarom lange blyven:</margin>
Zedert bragt de tolk *Phatfyofaymon* bericht: hoe 's Kaifars minne-moeder, door een fchielyke ziekte overvallen, te bedde lagh: waarom 't hof alle rechtzaken ftaakte, ter tydt men een weinig beterschap beooghde. Weshalven dan ook de *Hollanders* lydtzaamheit moeften hebben, indien als noch geen verlof verkreegen, om na *Nangefaque* te reizen.

<column-break/>

<margin>hebben bekkyk</margin>
Des anderen daags braghten *Manyckebe*, *Syovan*, *Kytsbyoye*, *Phatfyofaymon*, en de huis-waerdt, een merkelyk aantal *Japanders* op de kamer, alwaar de tien gevangene *Hollanders* by elkander zaten, buiten twyfel uit nieuwsgierigheidt. Deeze voerden onderling verfcheide redenen: welke by de *Hollanders*, alzoo *Japans* fpraken, niet verftaan wierden: alleenlyk hoorden zy nu en dan de naamen *Elferak* en *Overwater* melden. *Manyckebe* eindelyk vertaalde aan *Schaap*: dat een dezer vreemde *Japanders*, onlangs uit *Nangefaque* herwaards verreift, de heeren *Elferak*, *Overwater*, en vordere vrienden fprak, en aldaar in goede gezondheit liet. En geen ander befcheid quam uit *Manyckebes*; want als *Schaap* hem eenige vragen, wegens haar gevangenis, voor ftelde, weigerde hy te antwoorden, en wees hem met trotsheit af.

<margin>De Paauw wort dezer</margin>
Zedert hadden de *Hollanders* nu en dan zeer veel bekyks: en is de jongen *Jacob de Paauw*, door de zoon des Hollandtfchen huis-waerdt, na 't paleis van *Sicungodonne* geleidt: onder voorwending, hoe eenige Japanfche juffrouwen benieuwt waren om hem te zien. Doch zynde des avondts wederom te rugge gekomen, verhaalde hy: dat geen juffers zagh; maar wel *Sicungodonnes* opper-geheim-fchryver, nevens twee Duitfche tolken *Tofaymon* en *Manyckebe*: door welke onderzocht wierdt wegens het fchieten in d'inwyk *Namboe*: hoe veel maal het gefchut geloft was? En of de *Japanders* wel piftoolen en vuur-roers hadden afgebrandt? 't Antwoordt der jongen quam met het voorige over-een.

<margin>Eeder Jafaf Ryk Hol ver</margin>
Den negentienden van wyn-maandt hadden de vier tolken een t'zamenkomft in de Hollandtfche herberg: op haar kamer verfcheenen ook de tien gevangene *Hollanders*, die door *Tofaymon* bericht kreegen, om tegen morgen, een uur voor dag, haar gereed te houden: alzoo ten huize van *Sicungodonne*

Schaep and Byleveld now well observ'd what the reason was that the Interpreters kept themselves at such a distance with them, and still snapping at them, said, You relate Untruths before the Council: Therefore they humbly besought them, That Kytshyoge, Phatsyosamon, and Syovan, which now understood the Business, would take the trouble upon them, to intercede for them to the Lord Sicungodonne, for the Mistake which had been made by the Dutch Interpreters: Which Request they all three granted; and going from them, bid them be of good Courage.
And indeed they seem'd to be much concern'd [therein], for the next day they came again to the Hollanders Lodgings, where finding Manykebe, they told him, That he, and chiefly Tosaymon, had falsly interpreted for the Hollanders to the Council; and therefore it was high time that Manykebe his Brother were made acquainted therewith. But Manykebe laid all the fault on Tosaymon, at whose command, as being Chief Interpreter, he was forc'd to be silent. At last, the news thereof coming to Tosaymon's Ears, he neglected not to speak to the Hollanders concerning it; and excusing himself, said, That the fault was not in him, but Sicungodonne, he having faithfully translated Word for Word, which he sometimes told the Council quite contrary: Yet it appear'd sufficiently by Tosaymon's Countenance, that he was not without fault; therefore Schaep desired him, That for the future he would have a better care, and observe the Questions and Answers, that the Japan Council might come to a right and true understanding of the whole Business, and free them from further [delay]: Which he promising to perform, took his leave.
After this, the Interpreter Phatsyosamon brought them word, That the Emperors Mother was fallen exceeding sick; wherefore the Court would not hear any Causes whatsoever, till such time as she was recover'd: Therefore they must have a little longer Patience, if they got not leave to go for Nangesaque so soon as they expected.
The next day Manykebe, Syovan, Kitchyoge, Phatsyosamon, and their Landlord, brought a considerable number of Japanners into the Chamber where the ten Hollanders sat, which out of curiosity came to see them, holding a great Discourse amongst themselves, which the Hollanders (they speaking the Japan Tongue) could not understand; only they now and then heard them mention the Names Elserak and Overtwater: Manykebe at last interpreting to Schaep, said, That one of the Japanners there present was lately come thither from Nangesaque, and at his departure from thence, spoke with Mr. Elserak and Overtwater, and several other of their Countreymen, which he left all in good health; But no other Account would Manykebe give him, for when Schaep ask'd him any thing concerning their Releasment, he refus'd to answer, and scornfully commanded him to be silent.
Since this Visit, the Hollanders had many that came to see them, and the Youth Jacob de Paw was by their Landlords Son carried to Sicungodonne's Palace, under a pretence, that some Japan Ladies were desirous to see him: But returning at night, related, That he had seen no Ladies, but Sicungodonne's Secretary, and the Dutch Interpreters Tosaymon and Manykebe, who examin'd him concerning their Shooting in Nambo, and how often they fired? and if the Japanners discharg'd any Pistols or Firelocks on board of the Ship? All which the Youth answer'd as the rest had done before.
The nineteenth of October the four Interpreters had a Meeting in the Hollanders Inn, where the ten Dutch Prisoners were brought before them, and told by Tosaymon, That they should make themselves ready to morrow Morning, an Hour before Day-light, because a Meeting was agreed on by the Council at Sicungodonne's House to have another Hearing about their Business.

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page, Schaap and Byleveld seek to address the misinterpretations caused by the interpreters Tofaymon and Manyckebe.</meta>

*Schaap* and *Byleveldt* now noticed where the problem lay: that *Tofaymon* and *Manyckebe* kept themselves so separated from the *Dutchmen*, and only chided them: "You people misrepresent your words before the judges." Therefore, they humbly requested: whether *Kytsbyoye*, *Phatfyofaymon*, and *Syovan*, who now understood the matter correctly, would take the trouble to greet the lord *Sicungodonne* regarding the said error committed by the Dutch interpreters: a request which all three took very seriously. Departing, they gave the *Dutchmen* good courage.

<margin>Negotiation of the interpreters among themselves.</margin>
And the matter truly seemed to touch their hearts, for the next day they appeared again at the Dutch inn: where they found *Manyckebe*, whom they addressed: how he, and especially *Tofaymon*, had translated the *Dutchmen* very poorly before the Imperial Council: it was highly necessary that *Manyckebe* greet his colleague *Tofaymon* regarding this. But *Manyckebe* refused: as *Tofaymon* was the chief interpreter, to whom he had to yield. However, it reached *Tofaymon*'s ears: who did not fail to address the *Dutchmen* about the bad translation. He excused himself, saying that the fault was not his, but *Sicungodonne*'s: as he had faithfully translated word for word: although *Sicungodonne* sometimes conveyed the same to the Imperial Council entirely differently than what was said. Meanwhile, it appeared sufficiently from *Tofaymon*'s gestures that he was not without fault. *Schaap* therefore requested: that he would please take good care regarding the questions and answers in future examinations: so that the Japanese authorities might arrive at the true nature of the case, and they, the *Dutchmen*, encounter no further obstruction. He promised to do so, and departed.

<margin>Why the Dutch stay a long time:</margin>
Since then, the interpreter *Phatfyofaymon* brought word: how the Emperor's <note>original: "Kaifars"</note> mother, struck by a sudden illness, lay in bed: for which reason the court ceased all legal cases, until such time as one hoped for a little improvement. Wherefore the *Dutchmen* had to have patience, if they had not yet obtained permission to travel to *Nangefaque*.

<column-break/>

<margin>Many curious onlookers</margin>
The next day, *Manyckebe*, *Syovan*, *Kytsbyoye*, *Phatfyofaymon*, and the landlord brought a remarkable number of *Japanese* into the room where the ten imprisoned *Dutchmen* sat together, undoubtedly out of curiosity. They carried on various conversations among themselves: which were not understood by the *Dutchmen*, as they spoke *Japanese*: they only heard the names *Elferak* and *Overwater* mentioned now and then. *Manyckebe* finally translated for *Schaap*: that one of these strange *Japanese*, having recently traveled here from *Nangefaque*, spoke with the lords *Elferak*, *Overwater*, and other friends, and left them there in good health. And no other information came from *Manyckebe*; for when *Schaap* put some questions to him regarding their imprisonment, he refused to answer and dismissed him with arrogance.

<margin>Jacob de Paauw</margin>
Since then, the *Dutchmen* had a great many onlookers now and then: and the boy *Jacob de Paauw* was led by the son of the Dutch landlord to the palace of *Sicungodonne*: under the pretense that some Japanese ladies were curious to see him. But having returned in the evening, he reported: that he saw no ladies; but indeed *Sicungodonne*'s chief secretary, along with the two Dutch interpreters *Tofaymon* and *Manyckebe*: by whom he was examined regarding the shooting at the fort *Namboe*: how many times the artillery had been fired? And whether the *Japanese* had also fired pistols and muskets? The boy's answer agreed with the previous one.

<margin>Former Japanese Empire hollowness</margin>
On the nineteenth of October <note>original: "wyn-maandt"</note>, the four interpreters had a meeting in the Dutch inn: the ten imprisoned *Dutchmen* also appeared in their room, and received word from *Tofaymon* to keep themselves ready for tomorrow, an hour before daybreak: as at the house of *Sicungodonne*...

<summary>The Dutch prisoners attempt to resolve communication issues with their interpreters while waiting for the Imperial court to resume after the illness of the Emperor's mother. They are subjected to curious Japanese visitors and further questioning regarding their past actions.</summary>

# AAN DEN HOOG EDELEN WEL GEBOOREN HEERE,

->*Den Heer Frederik Adriaan, Baron van Rhede, Vry-Heer van Renswoude en Emmikhuyfen, Heer van Moerkerken, Gecommitteerde wegens de Provintie van Uytregt in het Collegie van de Hoog-Mogende Heeren Staten Generaal der Vereenigde Nederlanden.*<-

IN de maant van April ende Mey des Jaars 1716. wierd in onfe Stad overvloet van Schelvis gebragt, die ons van de Zee-dorpen Katwyk, Schevelinge, en Ter-Hey quamen: waar van veele onbeftorven waren, die wy Krimp-fchelvis noemen, ende op eenige dagen zoo goede koop waren, dat ze minder als een ftuyver het ftuk gekogt wierden. En fulks is ook voor eenige jaren voorgevallen.

Over de menigte van defe feer fmakelyke Schelvis, die men doen ter tyd met netten was vangende, daar die anders met aas die men aan een Vishoek doet gevangen wort, myn gedagten latende gaan; beelde ik my in, dat 'er een reden moeft wefen, waarom de Schelviffchen in fulken overvloet onfe Zee-kuften naderden; nademaal een maant ofte twee daar na geen eene Schelvis op onfe kuften gevangen wierde.

Ik beelde my felven in, dat de overvloet van de Schelviffchen was afhangende van het aas, ofte voetfel, dat ze op onfe Zee-kuften waren vindende.

An extraordinary quantity of Fish on the sea coast near Delft, noted by the Author, with the reasons assigned by him for the same.
In the months of April and May 1716, there were brought to our town of Delft, from the sea coasts at Schevling, Catwick, and Ter-Heid, a great quantity of the fish called haddocks, which, though very fresh and good, were sold at a low price. The glut of this fish was so great, that though in general they are caught with hooks, they were on this occasion, taken in nets.
Seeing this, I considered, that there must be some particular reason, why these fish should at that time resort to our coasts in such multitudes, and I was afterwards confirmed in that opinion, for in a month or two afterwards, not one of those fish was to be taken: and the reason which I assigned to myself for the abundance I have mentioned was, that at that time, there was a greater quantity of food for them on the coast than usual, whereby they had been tempted thither.

# TO THE HIGH NOBLE WELL-BORN LORD,

->*Lord Frederik Adriaan, Baron van Rhede, Free-Lord of Renswoude and Emmikhuyfen, Lord of Moerkerken, Commissioner on behalf of the Province of Utrecht in the College of the High and Mighty Lords States General of the United Netherlands.*<-

IN the months of April and May of the year 1716, an abundance of haddock was brought into our city, which came to us from the seaside villages of Katwijk, Scheveningen, and Ter Heij. Many of these were still alive <note>original: "onbestorven" — meaning recently caught and still fresh/twitching</note>, which we call "crimp-haddock" <note>original: "Krimp-schelvis"</note>, and on some days they were so cheap that they were bought for less than a stiver <note>a Dutch coin of low value</note> apiece. And such has also occurred in years past.

Reflecting upon the multitude of these very tasty haddock, which were caught at that time with nets, whereas they are otherwise caught with bait placed on a fishhook, I imagined that there must be a reason why the haddock approached our sea coasts in such abundance, since a month or two later, not a single haddock was caught on our coasts.

I imagined that the abundance of the haddock was dependent upon the bait, or food, that they were finding on our sea coasts.

In some places, where they ioyne, it is exceeding deepe, as in the Ilands of the South Sea, and in those of the North, whereas the shippes ride close to the land; and, although they found three score and tenne, yea foure score fadomes, yet do they finde no bottome, which makes men coniecture that these are pikes or poynts of land which rise vp from the bottome, a matter woorthy of great admiration. Heerevpon a very expert Pilote said vnto me, that the Ilands which they call of Woolves, and others, that lie at the entry of the coast of New Spaine, beeing called Cocos, were of this manner. Moreover, there is a place in the midst of the great Ocean, without the view of land, and many leagues from it, where are seene as it were two towers or pikes of a very high elevated rocke, rising out of the middest of the sea, and yet ioyning vnto it they finde no bottome. No man can yet perfectly comprehend, nor conceive the full and perfect forme of the land at the Indies, the boundes being not wholly discovered to this day: yet wee may guesse that it is proportioned like a heart with the lungs. The broadest of this heart is from Bresill to Peru, the poynt at the straight of Magellan, and the top where it ends is the firme land, and there the continent begins by little and litle to extend it selfe vntill wee come to the height of Florida and the vpper landes, which are not yet well discovered. We may vnderstand other particularities of this land at the Indies, by the Commentaries which the Spaniards have written of their successe and discoveries; and amongest the rest, of the Peregrination which I have written; which in trueth is strange, and may give a great light. This, in my opinion, may suffice at this time to give som knowledge of things at the Indies, touching the common elements, of the which all parts of the worlde are famed.
THE FOVRTH BOOKE of the Naturall and Morall Historie of the Indies.
Chap. i. — Of three kindes of mixtures or compounds, of the which I must intreate in this Historie.
Having intreated in the former booke of that which concernes the Elements, and the simples of the Indies, in this present booke we will discourse of mixtures and compounds, seeming fit for the subject we shall treate of. And although there be many other sundrie kindes, yet we will reduce this matter into three, which are Mettalls, Plants, and Beasts. Mettalls are (as plants) hidden and buried in the bowels of the earth, which have some conformitie in themselves, in the forme and maner of their production; for that wee see and discover even in them, branches, and as it were a bodie, from whence they grow and proceede, which are the greater veines and the lesse, so as they have a knitting in themselves: and it seemes properly that these minerales grow like vnto plants, not that they have any inward vegitative life, being onely proper to plants: but they are engendered in the bowels of the earth, by the vertue and force of the Sunne and other planets, and in long continuance of time they increase and multiply after the manner of plants. And even as mettalls be plants hidden in the earth, so we may say, that plants be living creatures fixed in one place, whose life is maintained by the nourishment which Nature furnisheth from their first beginning. But living creatures surpasse plants, in that they have a more perfect being; and therefore have neede of a more perfect foode and nourishment; for the search whereof, Nature hath given them a moving and feeling to discover and discerne it. So as the rough and barren earth is as a substance and nutriment for mettalls; and that which is fertile and better seasoned a nourishment for plants. The same plants serve as a nourishment for living creatures, and the plants and living creatures together as a nourishment for men; the inferiour nature alwaies serving for the maintenance and sustentation of the superiour, and the lesse perfect yeelding vnto the more perfect: whereby we may see how much it wants, that gold and silver and other things which men so much esteeme by their covetousnesse, should be the happiness of man, wherevnto he should tend, seeing they be so many degrees in qualitie inferior to man, who hath been created and made onely to be a subject to serve the vniversall Creator of all things, as his proper end and perfect rest, and to which man, all other things in this world, were not propounded or left, but to gaine this last end.

Thus far, then, the individual primary substances have been described to some extent; we shall now, for the present, likewise occupy ourselves a little with the mixed substances thereof. Although these now consist of four kinds, we want to divide them into three, namely, metals, plants, and animals.

<margin>Mineral substances of America described.</margin>
The metals are then like hidden plants rooted in the entrails of the earth, whose veins sprout like branches here and there, from which one can conclude that they grow like other offshoots and herbs. Not, however, that they truly have an sprouting life-force like herbs, but because they grow in the earth in this manner, and through the cooperation of the sun and other wandering stars <note>i.e., planets</note>, increase and ripen. Just as these metals are like hidden plants in the earth, so are they also like living creatures that, rooted in certain places, receive their nourishment from nature. Likewise, we find that the wild and barren earth provides nourishment for metals; where the fertile earth provides its growth to growing plants, plants to animals, and simultaneously plants and animals serve for the nourishment of mankind. Such is the unique nature for the preservation of the most worthy: what is not perfect is subject to the perfect. ### CAP. 22. Del principal Inga llamado Guaynacapa.

AL dicho Señor sucedio Guaynacapa, q̃ quiere dezir mãcebo rico o valeroso, y fue lo vno y lo otro, mas q̃ ninguno de sus antepassados ni sucessores. Fue muy prudente, y puso gran orden en la tierra en todas partes: fue determinado y valiente, y muy dichoso en la guerra, y alcançò grandes victorias. Este estendio su Reyno mucho mas que todos sus antepassados juntos: Tomole la muerte en el Reyno de Quito que auia ganado, que dista de su Corte quatrocientas leguas: Abrieronle, y las tripas, y el coraçõ quedaron en Quito, por auerlo el assi mãdado, y su cuerpo se traxo al Cuzco, y se puso en el famoso templo del Sol. Oy dia se muestran muchos edificios, y calçadas, y fuertes, y obras notables deste Rey: fundò la familia de Temebamba. Este Guaynacapa fue adorado de los suyos por dios en vida, cosa que afirmã los viejos que con ninguno de sus antecessores se hizo. Quando murio, matarõ mil personas de su casa, que le fuessen a seruir en la otra vida, y ellos morian con grã voluntad por yr a seruirle, tanto que muchos fuera de los señalados se ofrecian a la muerte para el mismo efecto. La riqueza y tesoro deste fue cosa no vista, y como poco despues de su muerte entrarõ los Españoles, tuuieron gran cuydado los Indios de desaparecerlo todo, aunq̃ mucha parte se lleuò a Caxamalca para el rescate de Atahualpa su hijo. Afirman hombres dignos de credito, que entre hijos y nietos tenia en el Cuzco mas de treziẽtos. La madre deste fue de grã estima: llamose Mamaoclo. Chap. xxii. — Of the greatest and most famous Ynca called Guaynacapa.

To this latter Ynca succeeded Guaynacapa, which is to say, a yoong man, rich and valiant, and so was he in trueth more than any of his predecessors, or successors. Hee was very wise, planting good orders thorowout his whole realme, hee was a bold and resolute man, valiant, and very happy in warre. Hee therefore obtained great victories, and extended his dominions much farther then all his predecessors had done before him; he died in the realme of Quito, the which he had conquered, foure hundred leagues distant from his court. The Indians opened him after his decease, leauing his heart and entrailes in Quito; the body was carried to Cusco, the which was placed in the renowmed temple of the Sunne. We see yet to this day many cawseries, buildings, fortresses, and notable workes of this king: hee founded the familie of Tumi-bamba. This Guaynacapa was worshipped of his subjects for a god, being yet alive, as the olde men affirme, which was not doone to any of his predecessours. When he died, they slew a thousand persons of his householde, to serve him in the other life, all which died willingly for his service, insomuch that many of them offered themselves to death, besides such as were appoynted: his riches and treasure was admirable. And forasmuch as the Spaniards entred soone after his death, the Indians laboured much to conceale all, although a great parte thereof was carried to Caxamarca, for the ransome of Atahualpa, his sonne. Some woorthy of credite affirme that he hadde above three hundred sonnes and grand-children in Cusco. His mother, called Mamaocllo, was much esteemed amongst them. Polo sent her body, with that of Guaynacapa, very well imbalmed, to Lima, rooting out infinite idolatries. To Guaynacapa succeeded in Cusco, a sonne of his called Titu-cusi-hualpa, who since was called Huascar Ynca; his body was burned by the captaines of Atahualpa, who was likewise sonne to Guaynacapa, and rebelled in Quito against his brother, marching against him with a mighty armie.

### CAP. 22. Of the principal <term>Inga</term> named <term>Guaynacapa</term>.

THE aforementioned Lord was succeeded by <term>Guaynacapa</term>, which means "rich or valiant youth," and he was both, more than any of his ancestors or successors. He was very prudent and put great order in the land in all places. He was determined and brave, and very fortunate in war, and achieved great victories. He extended his Kingdom much further than all his ancestors combined. Death overtook him in the Kingdom of Quito, which he had conquered, which is four hundred leagues from his Court. They opened him, and his entrails and heart remained in Quito, as he had so ordered, and his body was brought to Cuzco and placed in the famous temple of the Sun. To this day, many buildings, roads, fortresses, and notable works of this King are shown. He founded the family of Temebamba. This <term>Guaynacapa</term> was worshipped by his own people as a god while he was alive, a thing that the old men affirm was not done with any of his predecessors. When he died, they killed a thousand people from his house so that they might go to serve him in the other life, and they died with great willingness to go and serve him, so much so that many beyond those designated offered themselves to death for the same purpose. For if God makes known to anyone good or evil, relating to him or to others, and if the revelation thereof be founded on the obedience or disobedience of that person or the others, and if the facts continue the same, no doubt the prophecy will be fulfilled. But it is not, however, certain that it will be fulfilled in the letter, because the reasons of it may change. And therefore we must not trust to our own understanding of these revelations, but to faith.

CHAPTER XXI.
God is at times displeased with certain prayers, though He answers them. Illustrations of His anger with such prayers.

Some spiritual persons persuade themselves—not reflecting on the great curiosity which they often display when they seek knowledge from God in supernatural ways—because their prayers are sometimes answered, that their conduct in the matter is good and pleasing unto God. Nevertheless the truth is, notwithstanding the answers they receive, that God is offended, and not pleased. And more than this, they provoke Him to anger, and displease Him greatly. The reason is this—no creature may transgress the limits which God hath appointed in the order of its being for its rule and guidance. He has ordained for man's governance certain natural and reasonable laws, the transgression of which is therefore not right: now, to seek anything by supernatural ways is to transgress these laws, and therefore an unholy and unbecoming thing, and displeasing unto God.

SINCE, as we have said, some spiritual people are secure and do not pay much heed to the curiosity they sometimes use in trying to know certain things through supernatural means, thinking that because God sometimes answers their requests, it is a good term and that God likes it: however true it may be that He answers them, it is neither a good term, nor does God like it; rather, He dislikes it. And not only that, but He is often angry and feels it deeply. The reason for this is that it is not appropriate for any creature to go outside the terms that God has ordered for its government. He placed rational terms upon man for his government; therefore, wanting to go outside them, and wanting to ascertain and reach things through supernatural means, is to go outside one's terms. Therefore, it is not a holy or convenient thing; therefore, God does not like it. You will say: "If it is true that God does not like it, why does He sometimes answer?" I reply that sometimes the devil answers. But when God answers, I say it is because of the weakness of the soul, which wants to go along that path, so that it does not become discouraged and turn back, or so that it does not think that God is displeased with it, and thus be tempted too much, or for other ends that God knows are founded in the weakness of that soul, for which He sees that it is appropriate to answer and condescend along that path.

This being perceiued, I saide one day to my Lady, that it was the doctrine of Phisitions, that the medicines which doe not heale diseases, cannot preserue that we fall not into them, but that it seemed good to mee that wee shoulde giue vnto him euerie morning the pouder of the Bezaar stone, that with the continuall vse thereof, the vapour might bee consumed which did ryse vp to the braines, so that what seemeth to be venomous and hurtful, the stone would extinguish and kil, and would consume the vapour that riseth vp from all the body, and from some particular member, the roote and originall beeing taken away of the disease, he should bee healed: so euerie morning it was giuen him fasting the waight of three graines, of the pouder of the stone, with the water of Oxetongue, & it pleased God that it should worke so effectually, that from the day that he began to take it, vntil he died of another disease after, which was more then x. yeeres, there neuer came to him any soundings, the which stone he tooke vi. monethes together, and neuer missed day.

This effect being proued so great and manyfest, I hauing in cure a young Gentlewoman called the Lady Maria Catano, and was sicke of certaine soundings of long tyme, & beeing in cure by learned Phisitions, her disease of soundings was perillous for that it held her x. or xii. houres and those were well neere euerie day: she was in such case that many daies she rose not from her bed. I was called to cure her, seing the smal helpe that the other Phisitions had done to her, I did not meddle with the common medicines which other Phisitions had vsed many yeeres: but I caused to be brought from Lishebron a Bezaar stone, and after shee was purged, I gaue it her by the order aforesaide: and from the day that shee beganne to take it vnto this day shee neuer hadde more sowndinges, which is more then twelue yeares: there was spent a whole stone as great as a Date.

En ellas estuvo el desterrado Hancohuallu los postreros días que estuvo en su señorío, como despidiéndose de ellas, las cuales, según dicen sus indios, sintió más dejar que todo su estado. Sosegado el alboroto que causó la huida de Hancohuallu y acabada la visita que el Inca hacía de su Imperio, se volvió al Cozco, con determinación de hacer asiento por algunos años en su corte y ocuparse en el gobierno y beneficio de sus reinos hasta que se olvidase este segundo motín de los Chancas. Lo primero que hizo fue promulgar algunas leyes que parecieron convenir, para atajar que no sucediesen otros levantamientos como los pasados. Envió a las provincias chancas gente, de la que llamaban advenediza, en cantidad de diez mil vecinos, que poblasen y restaurasen la falta de los que murieron en la batalla de Yahuarpampa y de los que se fueron con Hancohuallu. Dióles por caudillos Incas de los del privilegio, los cuales ocuparon los vacíos que en aquellas provincias había.

Concluido lo que se ha dicho, mandó hacer grandes y suntuosos edificios por todo su Imperio, particularmente en el valle Yúcay, y más abajo, en Tampu. Aquel valle se aventaja en excelencia a todos los que hay en el Perú, por lo cual todos los Reyes Incas, desde Manco Cápac, que fue el primero, hasta el último, lo tuvieron por jardín y lugar de sus deleites y recreación donde iban a alentarse de la carga y pesadumbre que el reinar tiene consigo, con los negocios de paz y de guerra que perpetuamente se ofrecen. Está cuatro leguas pequeñas al nordeste de la ciudad; el sitio es amenísimo, de aires frescos y suaves, de lindas aguas, de perpetua templanza, de tiempo sin frío ni calor, sin moscas ni mosquitos ni otras sabandijas penosas. Está entre dos sierras grandes; la que tiene al levante es la gran cordillera de la Sierra Nevada, que con una de sus vueltas llega hasta allí. Lo alto de aquella sierra es de perpetua nieve, de la cual descienden al valle muchos arroyos de agua, de que sacan acequias para regar los campos. Lo medio de la sierra es de bravísimas montañas: la falda de ella es de ricos y abundantes pastos llenos de venados, corzos, gamos, huanacus y vicuñas y perdices, y otras muchas aves, aunque el desperdicio de los españoles tiene ya destruido todo lo que es cacería. Lo llano del valle es de fertilísimas heredades, llenas de viñas y árboles frutales y cañaverales de azúcar que los españoles han puesto.

La otra sierra que tiene al poniente es baja, aunque tiene más de una legua de subida; al pie de ella corre el caudaloso río de Yúcay, con suave y mansa corriente, con mucha pesquería y abundancia de garzas, ánades y otras aves de agua. Por las cuales cosas se van a convalecer a aquel valle todos los enfermos del Cozco que pueden ir a él, porque la ciudad, por ser de temple más frío, no es buena para convalecientes. El día de hoy no se tiene por bienandante el español morador del Cozco si no tiene parte en aquel valle. reference_text:
They also visited two famous fortresses, which in ancient times had belonged to the ancestors of Hanco-huallu, called Challcu-marca and Surumarca. Marca, in the language of these provinces, means a fortress. The exiled Hanco-huallu resided in one of them, during the last days that he remained in his own dominions, to take leave of them, for the Indians say that he felt leaving them more than the loss of all his estates besides. The excitement caused by the flight of Hanco-huallu having subsided, and the visit being finished which the Ynca made to all his provinces, Uira-ccocha resolved to remain some years in his court at Cuzco, and to employ his time in the administration of his kingdom until this second disturbance among the Chancas was forgotten. The first thing he did was to promulgate certain laws, the object of which appears to have been to prevent any such rebellion in future. He sent to the provinces of the Chancas ten thousand people, whom they called emigrants, to settle and supply the places of those who had fallen in the battle of Yahuar-pampa, and of those who had fled with Hanco-huallu. Yncas, by privilege, were appointed as their chiefs, and they filled up the void that had been left in those regions.

After having completed these arrangements, the Ynca commanded grand and sumptuous edifices to be built throughout his dominions, especially in the valley of Yucay, and lower down at Tampu. This valley excels all others in Peru for its many advantages; and all the kings Yncas, from the time of Manco Ccapac, who was the first, until the last, used it for a garden and place of recreation and enjoyment, to which they resorted when they wanted to throw off for a time the cares and anxieties of government. It is four short leagues north-east of the city. The climate is most agreeable, fresh, and soft, with constant fine weather, and free from heat and cold, flies and mosquitoes. It is situated between two ranges of lofty mountains, that to the east being the great chain of the snowy Andes, which, in one of its turns, reaches to this point. The tops of these mountains are covered with perpetual snow, whence many streams descend into the valley, and the water is taken off to irrigate the fields. Midway up the sides of the mountains there are thick forests, and at their feet are rich pastures abounding in deer, huanucos, vicunas, partridges, and many other birds, although nearly all the game has now been destroyed by the Spaniards. The bottom of the valley is covered with rich farms, consisting of vineyards, fruit-gardens, and fields of sugar-cane planted by the Spaniards.

The chain of hills to the westward is lower, though the ascent from the valley on that side is more than a league in length. At the foot of it flows the great river of Yucay, with a gentle current. It is full of fish, and abounds in herons, ducks, and other water-fowl. All the invalids of Cuzco go to the valley to enjoy these delights, for the city, being in a very cold climate, is not good for people recovering from illness. At the present day a Spanish inhabitant of Cuzco is not considered well off unless he also has a place in that valley. The Ynca Uira-Ccocha was especially fond of it, and ordered many edifices to be built there, some for recreation, and others to display his grandeur and magnificence.

The first thing he did was to promulgate some laws that seemed appropriate to prevent other uprisings like the past ones from occurring. He sent to the Chanca provinces people of the kind they called newcomers, in the number of ten thousand residents, to settle and restore the lack of those who died in the battle of Yahuarpampa and of those who went with Hancohuallu. He gave them as leaders Incas of the privileged class, who occupied the voids that existed in those provinces.

Having concluded what has been said, he ordered great and sumptuous buildings to be made throughout his Empire, particularly in the Yúcay valley, and further down, in Tampu. That valley surpasses in excellence all others that exist in Peru, for which reason all the Inca Kings, from Manco Cápac, who was the first, until the last, held it as a garden and place of their delights and recreation, where they went to be refreshed from the burden and heaviness that reigning carries with it, with the affairs of peace and war that perpetually offer themselves. It is four small leagues to the northeast of the city; the site is most pleasant, with fresh and gentle air, fine waters, of perpetual mildness, of weather without cold or heat, without flies or mosquitoes or other troublesome vermin. It is between two large mountain ranges; the one to the east is the great mountain range of the Sierra Nevada, which with one of its turns reaches as far as there. The top of that mountain range is of perpetual snow, from which descend to the valley many streams of water, from which they draw irrigation canals to water the fields. The middle of the mountain range consists of very wild mountains; the skirt of it consists of rich and abundant pastures full of deer, roe deer, fallow deer, <term>huanacus</term> <gloss>guanacos</gloss> and <term>vicuñas</term> <gloss>wild camelids</gloss> and partridges, and many other birds, although the wastefulness of the Spaniards has already destroyed everything that is game. The flat part of the valley consists of most fertile estates, full of vineyards and fruit trees and sugar cane fields that the Spaniards have planted.

The other mountain range that is to the west is low, although it has more than a league of ascent; at the foot of it runs the mighty river of Yúcay, with a soft and gentle current, with much fishing and abundance of herons, ducks, and other water birds. For these reasons, all the sick from Cozco who can go to it go to that valley to convalesce, because the city, being of a colder temperament, is not good for convalescents. The Spaniard living in Cozco today does not consider himself fortunate if he does not have a share in that valley. This Inca Viracocha was particularly fond of that site, and so he ordered many

### CAPIT. LXVI.

**Como otro dia embiamos mensajeros a los Caciques de Tlascala, rogandoles con la paz, y lo que sobre ello hizieron.**

Despues de passada la batalla por mi contada, que prendimos en ella los tres Indios principales, embiolos luego nuestro Capitan Cortes, y con los dos que estava en nuestro Real que avian ido otras vezes por mensajeros, les mando que dixessen a los Caciques de Tlascala, que les rogauamos, que vegan luego de paz, y que nos den passada por su tierra para ir a Mexico, como otras vezes les hemos embiado a dezir: e que si aora no vienen, que les mataremos todas sus gentes, y porque los queremos mucho, y tener por hermanos, no les quifieramos enojar, si ellos no huuessen dado causa a ello, y se les dixo muchos halagos para atraerlos a nuestra amistad: yaquellos mensajeros fueron de buena gana luego a la cabecera de Tlascala, y dixero su embaxada a todos los Caciques, por mi ya nombrados: los quales hallaron juntos con otros muchos viejos y Papas, y estauan muy tristes, ansi del mal suceso de la guerra, como de la muerte de los Capitanes parientes, o hijos suyos que en las batallas murieron, y dize que no les quifieron escuchar de buena gana; y lo sobre ello acordaron, fue, que luego mandaron llamar todos los adiuinos y Papas, y otros que echauan suerte, que llaman Tacalnagual, que son como hechizeros, y dixeron que mirassen por sus adiuinanzas y hechizos y fuertes, que gente eramos, y si podriamos fer vencidos dandonos guerra de dia y de noche a la contina, y tambien para saber si eramos Teules, ansi como lo dezian los de Cempoal, que ya he dicho otras vezes, que son cosas malas como demonios, e que cosas comiamos, e que mirassen todo esto con mucha diligencia: y despues que se juntaron los adiuinos, y hechizeros, y muchos Papas, y hechas sus adiuinanzas, y echadas sus fuertes, y todo lo que folian hazer; parece fer, dixeron, que en las fuertes hallaron, que eramos hombres de hueffo y de carne, y que comiamos gallinas, y perros, y pan, uinos de los y fruta quando lo teniamos, y que no comiamos carnes de Indios, ni corazones de los que marauamos, porque segun parecio, los Indios amigos que traiamos de Cempoal, les hizieron encreyente que eramos Teules, e que comiamos corazones de Indios, e que las bombardas echauan rayos como caen del cielo, e que el lebrel, que era tigre o leon, y que los cauallos eran para lancear a los Indios quando los queriamos matar; y les dixeron otras muchas niñerias. E boluamos a los Papas, y lo peor de todo, que les dixeron sus Papas e adiuinos, fue, que de dia no podiamos fer vencidos, sino de noche, porque como anochecia se nos quitauan las fuerças: y mas les dixeron los hechizeros, que eramos esforçados, y que todas estas virtudes teniamos de dia hasta que ponia el Sol, y desque anochecia no teniamos fuerças ningunas. Y quando aquello oyeron los Caciques, y lo tuuieron por muy cierto, se lo embiaron a dezir a su Capitan General Xicotenga, para que luego con breuedad venga vna noche con grandes poderes a nos dar guerra. El qual como lo supo juto obra de diez mil Indios los mas esforçados que tenia, y vino a nuestro Real, y por tres partes nos comeco a dar vna mano de flechas, y tirar varas con sus tiraderas de vn gajo y de dos, y los de espadas y macanas, y motantes por otra parte, por manera, que de repente tuuieron por cierto, que lleuarian algunos de nosotros para sacrificar; y mejor lo hizieron nuestro Señor Dios, que por muy fecretamente que ellos venian, nos hallaron muy apercebidos; porque como fintiero su gran ruido que traian a matacuallo, vinieron nuestros corredores del campo, y las espias a dar al arma; y como estauamos tan acostumbrados a dormir calçados, y las armas vestidas, y los cauallos enfillados, y enfrenados, y todo genero de armas muy a punto, les refistimos con las escopetas y ballestas, y eltocadas de presto bueluen las espaldas, y como era campo llano, y hazia luna
